title: France beat Argentina to set up Nations Championship final with South Africa - The Guardian
content: England face All Blacks rematch in third-place game France and South Africa will contest the inaugural Nations Championship grand final next Sunday in London, while England will face an immediate rematch with the All Blacks next Saturday. Les Bleus defeated Argentina 45-17 in Paris, ultimately overwhelming the Pumas with five second-half tries and seven overall at the Stade de France. They confirmed top spot in the northern hemisphere table with the required bonus-point win, finishing on 26 points with five wins out of six. England (five bonus points) and Ireland (four bonus points) also won five matches, but finish second and third respectively. Friday 27 NovemberEleventh-place final Italy v Fiji 4.40pmFifth-place final Ireland v Australia 8.10pm Saturday 28 NovemberNinth-place final Wales v Japan 1.10pmThird-place final England v New Zealand 4.40pm Sunday 29 NovemberSeventh-place final Scotland v Argentina 1.10pmNations Championship final France v South Africa 4.40pm The Springboks were earlier defeated 20-17 by Ireland in Dublin, but securing a losing bonus point allowed the world champions to draw level on 22 points with New Zealand, and finish top of the southern hemisphere table with a vastly superior points difference, +135 to +41. South Africa and New Zealand both won four matches in six rounds. In Cardiff, at the same time as France’s win, Australia ended a four-match losing streak with a 29-26 success against Wales, clinching third place in the southern hemisphere table and setting up a finals weekend clash against Ireland next Friday. England had gone top of the northern table after a dominant 37-12 win against New Zealand at Twickenham earlier, but will now face the same opponents next Saturday evening, having been demoted to second by France. Before Friday’s Ireland v Australia game in the fifth-place final, Italy and Fiji, bottom in the north and south tables, will meet to avoid the wooden spoon in the inaugural championship. Scotland v Argentina (fourth v fourth) kicks off at 1.10pm next Sunday, before the grand final, while Wales v Japan (fifth v fifth) will begin 24 hours earlier, the first match of a double-header before England v New Zealand. Fiji produced a second-half fightback to end a run of five straight Nations Championship defeats with a 21-16 win over their fellow strugglers Italy in Udine. Italy – who had also lost all five of their previous games to sit bottom of the Northern Hemisphere table – took a 13-7 lead into half-time after a converted try from Lorenzo Cannone and two penalties from Tommaso Allan. Fiji, who came into Saturday’s match without a point, fought back early in the second half with a try from Tevita Ikanivere, his second in the game, and Caleb Muntz added the extras to put them in front. Kitione Salawa went over for Fiji’s third try of the match (pictured) in the 51st minute and although Allan slotted another penalty to give Italy some hope, there was no grandstand finish. Both sides are set to meet again at Twickenham over finals weekend, when they will play-off for 11th place overall. PA In Paris, Kalvin Gourgues scored two of the seven French tries against Argentina, who had the prop Mayco Vivas sent off in the second half, with the hooker Julián Montoya also sent to the sin-bin late on. Louis Bielle-Biarrey, the prolific Bordeaux Bègles wing, scorched across the try-line for the concluding try two minutes from time to seal a crushing win. Mickaël Guillard, Peato Mauvaka, Émilien Gailleton and Tyler Duguid scored the other tries for France while Justo Piccardo and Pablo Matera, after a late interception, scored Argentina’s tries. In next Sunday’s grand final, Rassie Erasmus’s South Africa will have the opportunity to avenge their 21-19 defeat by France in Paris this month. Erasmus will be absent from Twickenham after the head coach was banned for six matches by World Rugby for suggesting that officials in the defeat by France eight days ago had been “match-fixing”.

title: Wales v Wallabies: Five takeaways as 'ridiculous' Rees-Zammit stars in defeat to 'clinical' Australia - Planet Rugby
content: Wales wing Louis Rees-Zammit impressed in defeat to Australia. Following a 29-26 victory for Australia over Wales in the Nations Championship, here’s our five takeaways from the Principality Stadium. A lung-busting game that was a fantastic watch with eight tries scored and drama aplenty as Australia clung on to pick up a much-needed triumph. The result secures third place on the Southern Hemisphere table for the Wallabies while Wales finish in fifth position in the Northern Hemisphere. Tries from Taniela Tupou, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau were complemented by points off the tee from Ryan Lonergan and Carter Gordon as the Wallabies ended a run of four straight losses to release some of the pressure on both the players and Les Kiss’ coaching staff. Wales, whose tries came via Dewi Lake (2), Blair Murray and Ryan Elias, could not back up last weekend’s famous win over the All Blacks, but it wasn’t for a lack of trying, which is a credit to both the Wallabies’ resolve in defence and an ultra-clinical edge in attack as they ended the recent drought. One of the words to sum up the Wallabies’ performance tonight, for sure. They took their opportunities when they came and showed much more steel. Springboks v France rematch: Nations Championship finals weekend fixtures confirmed Wales will wonder how they were 12-0 adrift with 39 minutes played, this after they’d had 10 entries into the Australian 22 for no reward on the board. While the Welsh did cross late on in the opening half, a theme in Cardiff was the Wallabies scoring with the majority of their opportunities they had. All of their tries were lethal in their execution, and that will delight head coach Kiss, particularly after a hugely disappointing spell on their travels. Two moments of ridiculous quality from Louis Rees-Zammit that were largely due to the raw pace he possesses; he is simply a joy to watch right now. The first came during the opening period and it was in some respects comical, with the television commentator greeting the Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii intercept with 60 metres to go with the line “you are not stopping him”. Two seconds later – and with 40 metres remaining to the whitewash – the Welsh winger had the Wallaby centre wrapped up in a tackle. It was astonishing speed from Rees-Zammit that had to be seen to be believed. That was without the ball and in the second half we were treated to Rees-Zammit’s quality with ball in hand, as he skinned both Harry Potter and Suaalii with barely any room to work with in a moment that led to Murray scoring a critical match-leading try on 54 minutes to make it 21-19. Just a special talent who looks physically more powerful than ever, whilst not losing a step of his electric speed and he is all the more confident for it. Ikitau is fast becoming the crucial cog in this Wallabies line-up, such is the box of tricks he brings and how it benefits those team-mates around him. His amazing footwork, power in contact, soft hands and how he’s a perfect foil to both Gordon and Suaalii make him vital to the Wallabies’ midfield. Wallabies player ratings: Len Ikitau ‘shows his class’ alongside ‘promising’ Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii Ikitau was named Player of the Match at the Principality Stadium and rightly so, with the Wallabies a distinctly lesser outfit without him at No. 12. A third-place finish in their Nations Championship group means Australia will take on Ireland next Friday in what will be a testing fixture for the team in gold. The Irish are riding high after their victory over the Springboks and look in fine touch at the moment, so Australia must improve further. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Wales meanwhile will face Japan in Saturday’s opening game in a game that will prove how much they have grown in recent weeks. Remember, the Welsh could only eke out a 28-21 victory over the Brave Blossoms on November 7, so will strive for a more handsome winning margin at Twickenham. title: France v Argentina: Five takeaways as Les Bleus' brilliance overshadowed by 'biggest' worry for Springboks rematch - Planet Rugby
content: Louis Bielle-Biarrey of France celebrates and an inset of Fabien Galthie. Following France’s 45-17 victory over Argentina in Paris, here are our five takeaways from the Nations Championship clash. Les Bleus scored seven tries to top the northern conference and reach next weekend’s Nations Championship final, but a pack beasted for long spells will worry Fabien Galthié before South Africa. If last week’s win over the Springboks was a ten out of ten, this was about a four at best, and for the first half-hour that felt generous. France spent the opening 40 minutes running off the Pernod from last week, whilst Argentina, ferocious and beautifully organised, had the ball for almost the whole spell between the fifth and 25th minutes, won the collisions, won in the air, beasted France on the floor and shoved them around at the scrum; the Pumas had 62 per cent of the first-half possession, and France led 14-10 at the break on two scores built from very little ball. Only France can play that badly and then produce what came after the break; they scored five second-half tries, finished with seven to two and took the bonus point that puts them top of the northern conference and into the final against South Africa at Allianz Stadium next Sunday, which in turn sends England into the second-place match against New Zealand on Saturday. The difference, as so often, was the backline. France had fewer rucks, 71 to 92, carried 456 metres to 275, conceded fewer penalties and made 18 visits to the 22 to Argentina’s six, but Argentina won the kicking metres, 694 to 513, and turned France over seven times to three, and that last column should worry Galthié most with the Springboks next. Springboks v France rematch: Nations Championship finals weekend fixtures confirmed Make no mistake, the worry is up front. Jean-Baptiste Gros withdrew before the game, as Planet Rugby revealed, and will miss the rest of the campaign, and his absence was felt from the first scrum; Rodrigue Neti was crumpled more than once, Argentina twice turned down kicks to the corner or the posts to scrummage again because they were winning them, France melted the Argentine scrum once just after the break and got nothing for it, and they were so poor up front that they only looked marginally competitive on the tight when the scrums went uncontested late on, after Mayco Vivas’s red card and a pair of HIAs. The maul is a recurring pattern now and another big concern. Against Fiji, four second-half mauls went nowhere as France dropped the ball time and time again, and here the catcher stayed too high and the whole pack drove too high with him, so France never got a real percussive shove on; they were held up over the line, dropped the ball off a corner lineout, and it took several stalled drives before Peato Mauvaka finally went over on 33 minutes. It is almost as if they’re hitting the drive before the catcher has come down- over anxious, perhaps? On the floor, with François Cros rested, France had no ruck specialist and missing the man who owns the collisions and bosses the contact. As a result Argentina won seven turnovers, Facundo Isa and Rodrigo Isgró among the stealers. Maul, breakdown and scrum; those are precisely South Africa’s strengths, and losing Gros, a world-class loosehead, makes the scrum the biggest worry of all. There was credit too, mind you, for Esteban Capilla, who made 19 tackles on his first Test start, more than anyone on the pitch. Comment: England show All Blacks and Springboks do not ‘hold a monopoly on emotion’ as New Zealand ‘taken apart’ Here’s the thing about France: they don’t need long to strike once they have the ball. Kalvin Gourgues was player of the match and it’s fair to say a superstar was born in Paris in this match. With 96 metres, more than anyone else, three clean breaks, two tries and all five conversions, he was magnificent. His first, at 46 minutes, came from a moment of pure Matthieu Jalibert, a double pump and show that froze the defence for Gourgues to come through on a short line, exquisite from a fly-half who’d been OK rather than razor-sharp on his first start since September. Gourgues’ second was a 45-metre sprint down the left touchline after Tyler Duguid’s carry, a Florian Verhaeghe chicken-wing offload, Maxime Lucu’s quick hands and a pass from Louis Bielle-Biarrey, at the end of which Gourgues landed full on his own crown jewels and spent the next few minutes walking like a man who regretted his try-scoring choices. Bielle-Biarrey, la trottinette électrique, carried 14 times, more than anyone, and finished with two try assists for France and one for Argentina, throwing a pass straight to Pablo Matera, who ran it in at 71 minutes; he also finished off Antoine Dupont’s magical flick kick over the back of a scrum at 77 minutes for his 31st try in 30 Tests. Dupont threw 59 passes with two try assists; the returnees all went well: Anthony Jelonch with 11 tackles and a turnover and Charles Ollivon with 11 tackles and the early hit that forced Bautista Delguy off, and Grégory Alldritt was a one-man bomb squad off the bench whose run made Duguid’s try. One moment worth mentioning: at 66 minutes, came the most French moment of the night. Lucu, driven back over his own line, simply refused to put it down, offloaded to Théo Attissogbé who sidestepped through, Jefferson Poirot smashed it up and Cameron Woki and Gourgues tore down the left, 70 metres from their own in-goal, until Julián Montoya came off his feet to take out Dupont and was sent to the bin. Jouer, jouer. Ireland v Springboks: Five takeaways as bomb squad ‘diffused’ and ‘weaker scrum’ wins the day elsewhere Argentina deserved more than the scoreline suggests. Gerónimo Prisciantelli’s line made Justo Piccardo’s try, Tomás Albornoz ran the game for long spells, and this was a far more physical Pumas side than the one that has drifted through parts of the campaign. Davidson’s interpretation at the ruck demanded a very clear lift before she’d reward a jackler, which made life hard for both sides on the floor, and Argentina, ferocious there, went past the ruck a few times too many before she called the penalty. Her best decision came at 58 minutes, when Matera ran across in front of Jalibert and Jalibert then took Prisciantelli out in the air; she went back to Matera’s run first, calmly and accurately, and France had the penalty rather than a card. Vivas’s yellow for a tucked shoulder to Maxime Lamothe’s head was upgraded to red by the bunker, a surprise given how much was going on but reckless all the same, and with Montoya in the bin Argentina were down to 13 for a spell. The closing minutes descended into a bit of a farce over the HIA paperwork, and Davidson was the one who sorted it. England v All Blacks: Five takeaways as ‘wonderfully’ un-English performance delivers historic victory Galthié has some serious selection issues before then. The returnees were great, Jalibert, Jelonch and Ollivon all giving him reasons to keep them, but losing Gros leaves a hole in the front row he can’t simply pick his way out of; Cros surely has to come back to own the collisions, and the maul needs fixing in a week against the Springboks of all sides. So France meet South Africa in the final on Sunday, and on this evidence they’ll get minced, because this version of France is weak exactly where the Springboks are strong. In some ways, England, after demolishing New Zealand, and with a massive pack, would be the side to beat South Africa next week, but they’ll have the All Blacks again on Saturday instead, with the chance to beat them three times in a row for the first time. title: England v All Blacks: Winners and losers as Lee Blackett's signature glows on Twickenham turf - Planet Rugby
content: England v All Blacks: Winners and losers as Lee Blackett's signature glows on Twickenham turf England defeated the All Blacks 37-12 at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, in one of the most complete performances under Steve Borthwick’s reign. The Harlequins winger was a late call-up to the starting XV, but he certainly made the most of his unexpected opportunity. With Will Joseph moved to right wing, Cadan Murley settled on the left but played much of his game through the middle, providing a real attacking threat off the shoulders of Fin Smith and Seb Atkinson. He’s certainly in the mix for starting wingers, but having found Joseph catapulted in front of him, with this performance, he’s certainly shown Borthwick that he’s still very much in the fight. England’s attack purred, and that has to be down to Lee Blackett’s brilliance. This autumn, the squad are finally looking like a Blackett attack. The lines are being run to perfection, with the right angles, speed and intensity, and the All Blacks simply could not handle it. Much was made of Blackett’s arrival last year, but now finally the promise is being fulfilled. England finally seem to have a reliable, working midfield axis. Smith, Atkinson and Henry Slade all worked in expert tandem, in a midfield that felt like it truly clicked. Both Slade and Atkinson well deserved their tries, and again Smith controlled the game excellently throughout. If anyone can remember the last time Ben Earl had a genuinely bad game, we’d like to meet them. 33 carries, 8 defenders beaten and 138 metres made, he doubled the stats of his nearest challenger on each one. Totally deserved his try. To think it took him so long to establish himself as England’s first-choice full-back is bizarre, particularly considering the consistency with which he performs in the 15 jersey. Against New Zealand, he threatened every time he touched the ball, whether with his electric running game, fluid passing or clever kicking. The most understated part of his game is his reliability in defence, and once again he cleaned up every time the All Blacks threatened. Jamie George and co created a solid platform for the England attack to work off. Each time the ball landed, England were straight into the attack with a ferocity that kept the All Blacks on the back foot. Many questioned why the England boss was still in charge at the start of the Nations Championship, but he’s now quite clearly justified it. Following the match, Dave Rennie said “Steve’s done a good job turning it around”, and he’s not wrong. This England group, and their coach, are maturing at the perfect time, leading into the World Cup year. All Blacks: Jordie Barrett’s blunt admission on ‘incredibly tough moment’ from 2023 World Cup final For all his brilliance in attack, he resembled a revolving door in defence. Although Jordie Barrett and Damian McKenzie also missed four tackles, none were as obvious or as humiliating as his effort on Earl, when he was run over like a slow plough on ice. Perhaps unfair to highlight one man for England’s disappointing early scrum, but Fin Baxter looked to struggle against the All Black pack. He performed admirably against the Wallabies a couple of weeks ago, but his lack of match fitness sadly showed today. Confirmed just an hour before the game to have a knock which he couldn’t shake, the Northampton Saints winger wasn’t able to take part in what became a historic match for the national side. His spot in the team certainly won’t be in danger, but to miss such a brilliant match will hurt. The once mighty All Blacks looked utterly shattered out there. Barely able to launch any sort of assault of their own, they languished behind a scoreline that quite frankly flattered them. They were second best to every collision, made numerous uncharacteristic mistakes, and generally looked like a side that had mentally clocked out a couple of weeks ago. For all his star quality, he failed to sparkle in Twickenham, finding himself limited on space and short of ideas. Jordan was arguably one man who could pull New Zealand from the depths of defeat, but he never had the opportunity. His team failed to get him into the game, and his usual ability to navigate his way into the important areas simply wasn’t visible. Having Jordan on the field was like owning an Aston Martin in London city centre. title: Ireland v Springboks: Five takeaways as bomb squad 'diffused' and 'weaker scrum' wins the day elsewhere - Planet Rugby
content: Robert Baloucoune dives over for one of his two Ireland tries and, inset, South Africa No.10 Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu  (Charles McQuillian and Evan Treacy/Nations Championship/Getty Images) After a deserved 20-17 win for three-try Ireland over two-try South Africa, Planet Rugby picks out five takeaways from the gripping Nations Championship round six match. After all the histrionics of a dramatically controversial week in which the name of the banned Rassie Erasmus was on everyone’s lips, a superb rugby match swiftly broke out in Dublin on Saturday evening that bristled from start to finish and ended with Ireland defiantly holding on for a three-point triumph. A scrum penalty – what else? – opened the scoring, Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu firing over, but Ireland weren’t in the slightest rattled, hitting back with an eighth-minute Robert Baloucoune try on penalty advantage from a Stuart McCloskey assist. Eight minutes later, the home crowd was celebrating again, but this joy was short-lived as Cameron Hanekom had brilliantly dislodged the ball from Baloucoune’s grasp in the act of grounding. It was only a temporary South Africa reprieve, though. Damian Willemse’s deflection resulted in Mack Hansen regathering and throwing a basketball-style assist to Baloucoune to dive in at the corner on 19 minutes for 10-3. Aviva Stadium went wild. Those cheers were wilder still when a 26th-minute scrum penalty was won on a South Africa feed near the halfway line, but the shot of adrenaline didn’t equate to Irish points, the scoreboard next moving to the sound of South African points. A clever Canan Moodie kick ahead after some lovely Kurt-Lee Arendse dancing resulted in Hugo Keenan conceding a five-metre scrum, and the three minutes of pressure ended with Morne van den Berg touching down on 35 minutes with an eight-man shove having penalty advantage. Feinberg-Mngomezulu’s conversion seemed set to leave it deadlocked at 10-all at the interval, but a fabulous lineout drill ended with Ronan Kelleher showing Moodie he can boogie as well. Sam Prendergast’s extras left Ireland 17-10 up and thriving. Further nourishment for their soul came four minutes into the second half when Hansen did enough to scrag Moodie, who had steamrolled Jamison Gibson-Park, into touch when grounding over the try line. A 54th-minute Prendergast penalty after Joe McCarthy pressure stretched it to a 10-point gap that was reduced to three four minutes with Malcolm Marx’s close-range converted try. We were now down deep into an exhilarating battle of inches. Of significance was Feinberg-Mngomezulu holding Dan Sheehan up over the line on 62 minutes, and then came the 73rd-minute double yellow card incident; Sheehan and Marco van Staden binned for clear-outs at the same breakdown. The grind was intoxicating. Sub Nick Timoney’s carry from a five-metre scrum under is posts was especially gutsy, and especially daft was Jan-Hendrick Wessels illegal carry at a ruck before it all ended with Jesse Kriel’s knock-on. Well played, Ireland. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Too much hatred exists for the scrum when it should be a rugby calling card that must be celebrated, as was the case at Aviva Stadium. The crowd was loudly invested in every scrum and it was a joy to watch. The tally at the finish read four scrum penalties awarded to South Africa along with two frees, while they also scored their only first-half try from an eight-man shunt that had penalty advantage. In response, Ireland won one scrum penalty and two frees, the type of belligerence that demonstrated that while you can be in trouble in this set-piece, there is no reason it should cost you the result if you battle cleverly in other facets of play. The French highlighted this mission possible last weekend when they defeated the Springboks in Paris, but the Irish scrum was a better unit than the demolished Les Bleus one. What best summed up this intriguing battle was the effect of what took place heading towards the Dublin interval. A year ago, South Africa took Ireland to the hurt locker and resulting overlapping yellow cards certainly didn’t assist the wounded home team’s cause. Here, the Irish found themselves having to defend a five-metre scrum after Keenan carried back over his line. They survived that part of the pressure, but when South Africa got another scrum five metres out a few minutes later, Ireland wisely cut their losses on penalty advantage and allowed the visitors to score without interference. It ensured there was no yellow card coming, and Ireland’s pluck, unlike November 2025, saw them quickly go downfield after the restart and score. The scrum was a wonderful, hard-fought spectacle, but the salutary lesson following on from Stade de France was that the team with the weaker set-piece won the day elsewhere. Has muted Rassie Erasmus breached his World Rugby ban as Springboks boss delivers first-half verdict All year we have been hearing stellar reports about South Africa’s supposed imperiousness in the Test game, but this loss was the first time they have lost two on the bounce on Erasmus’ watch and it surely means that next year’s Rugby World Cup isn’t the predictable three-peat so many of the Boks’ fans believe it will be. South Africa will still contest next weekend’s Nations Championship final and so are still in a position to quickly add a trophy to their glittering collection, but the reality they can’t turned a blind eye to is they have been beaten four times now in their last eight matches. That is hardly the form of an undisputed world’s best team. As was the case in the France last weekend, they trailed at the break and didn’t have the cunning plan to rectify the situation. Amongst their first half issues was the lack of standout ball carriers. For instance, seven Irish names topped the interval carry list before a South African name cropped up, illustrating the pressure they had come under, and the top three places were still all Ireland’s at full-time despite securing more sufficient possession and territory to finish at full-time with overall 48 per cent possession and 49 per cent territory. Also, despite their scrum prowess, the full match penalty count ended 11-8 against Erasmus side, and it didn’t help that their feted ‘bomb squad’ had about as much impact those laughed at scud missiles in the Gulf War many years ago and was diffused. Wessels is touted as an alternative to Marx when needed but he didn’t cover himself in any glory here. His first lineout throw was a crooked as an Irish drunk walking home after the post-game part, and the penalty he gave up for illegally taking the ball at the ruck smacked of someone who doesn’t yet have the composure to be reliable at this level. Van Staden’s yellow was a further example of the bomb squad not delivering value and rather than blaming the world and its mother for its failings, it’s high time the Springboks took a long, lingering look in the mirror as themselves and realise they are not as fantastic as they have been made out to be in 2026. Springboks player ratings: Marco van Staden’s ‘brain fade’ proves costly as Bomb Squad implodes Welcome back to the top tier, Ireland. Andy Farrell’s team has been dogged by too much inconsistency for quite some time, and the anxious feeling after an unconvincing Southern Series was that the potency they once had some years ago had been diluted and wouldn’t be back any time soon. How wrong that consensus was, as a revved-up Irish side produced their best performance since the 2024 win in Durban. We’re not forgetting how tasty they were when filleting England last February in London, but this victory was some levels above and will go a long way towards restoring the faith that was lost in Project Farrell. The drop-off in overall form was among the reasons why the stadium wasn’t sold out the past two weekends, but the display conjured up against South Africa will reignite the demand for tickets for all matches, not just the big ones against the best teams in the world. We couldn’t get enough of McCarthy’s nuisance value at lock. It was his early hard carrying that asked serious questions, unlike what transpired a year ago when the teams last played each other, while Ryan Baird was another to put in a humongous shift. Farrell also executed a decent plan regarding the involvement of Prendergast – he wasn’t left vulnerable to hungry Boks. And then there was the menace of Baloucoune, who scored two first-half tries in the same corner and had another in-field ruled out for a fumble at the line. The winger’s aerial brilliance was also an important influence on the success. Ireland player ratings: ‘All-action’ wing rules the air while Joe McCarthy a ‘colossus’ as Springboks stunned Walking down Lansdowne Lane outside the stadium about three hours before kick-off, a man had emerged with a big sweeping brush to clear away some fallen leaves. It could have been a metaphor for Ireland’s gamble with Sheehan getting swept away by a Springboks onslaught, but it instead turned out that Farrell knew damn well what he was doing with the positional gambit. A world-class player suited to No.8 was how Farrell surmised his bet-the-house punt on shifting his hooker to back row for a first-time start in that role. Injuries to Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and James McNabney, as well as Nick Timoney’s unconvincing audition last weekend versus Fiji, convinced him it was the right way to go, and he was proven correct. Ireland needed a hard carrier at the back of the scrum and Sheehan was quick to take the ball and run twice in the opening 23 minutes rather than allow Springboks scrum pressure to build. Patrolling a different channel to what he was used to, there was a classy example of his skill early in the second half when he tidied up a kick and executed a super one-handed pass out of the follow-up tackle. In the end, despite an absence for a HIA and also a yellow card clear out, he made 31 metres off his 12 carries, eclipsing the impact made by Hanekom, his rival rookie No.8, who was handed the South African role due to Jasper Wiese’s suspension. The Springbok deserves credit for the way he denied Baloucoune a try and outscored Sheehan on the head-to-head tackle count 17 to 14. However, Ireland got way more out of their rookie No.8 than the visitors, and it had an influence on the round six result. content: Sam Prendergast and Ireland celebrate against South Africa. Ireland finished their Nations Championship group stage campaign on a high as they beat the Springboks 20-17 at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin. title: Match Report: All Blacks v England | Nations Championship, 2026 - All Blacks
content: The loss also took the potential chance to play in the final of the Nations Championship out of the All Blacks' hands, leaving it dependent on the result of the Ireland-South Africa Test. Two lost lineouts by the All Blacks in the first two minutes of the second half summed up their issues and helped seal their defeat. But they weren’t the only transgressions by a team looking to rebound from their Welsh humiliation of a week earlier. They were met on attack by a more determined athletic combination, whose defence blunted nearly every New Zealand thrust. New Zealand couldn’t make any impression in the loose where England dominated the breakdowns 136-65, and they used it well to beat 35 All Blacks defenders while New Zealand managed only 15. Instead of being an assured source of possession, the lineout became a handicap, with England picking off at least three throws at crucial stages and the All Blacks managing only 67 per cent success. England enjoyed utter domination of the first half, represented by their 19-5 lead, with 71 per cent possession and 78 per cent territory, and little changed in the second half, where they had 64 and 74 per cent, respectively. While they scored three tries to New Zealand’s one, they could have scored more as the All Blacks were too often penetrated when England ran the ball from the middle field. By the end, they had five tries to two, the basis of a record winning margin over New Zealand, who also suffered consecutive victories for the second time. Building momentum at speed, England ran hard onto the ball to stress the All Blacks’ defence but missed at least three chances that could have extended their lead. England ran 578 metres to 313 by the All Blacks and 173 carries to 108. But England made only 117 tackles, compared to 224 by New Zealand. Again, the now-regular penalties in the opening stages gifted England opportunities too easily. Their first came in the fifth minute when first five-eighths Fin Smith slipped a grubber kick into the in-goal area, and centre Henry Slade had the speed to get to the ball first. By 23 minutes, England had failed to take three scoring chances as the All Blacks exerted pressure in defence. But when New Zealand got chances to spend time in England’s half, they made errors that gave England breathing space. Halfback Cam Roigard’s kicks from the base of rucks were imprecise, often too long, and allowed England to charge back into the All Blacks’ half. Passing also lacked authority as seven handling mistakes were made, the last by prop Fletcher Newell. From a scrum 15 metres out, England No8 and man of the match Ben Earl ran from the back, beat Roigard’s tackle attempt and took England to a 19-0 lead in the 36th minute. Five minutes earlier, halfback Jack van Poortvliet leapt over a goalmouth ruck to be awarded a try. It showed how much New Zealand’s infringements and faults contributed to their scoreboard deficit when, from a 38th-minute lineout after a penalty, the ball was finally produced effectively. Hooker Codie Taylor ran off the back of the maul, and when tackled, prop Ethan de Groot got the ball over the line for some relief at last. A 42nd-minute lineout loss saw England work their chess-type support game up to the All Blacks' 22m area, where flanker Ollie Chessum scored. The All Blacks responded with their only positive move when Taylor made an initial burst, with lock Fabian Holland charging ahead to give the ball to Roigard, who found Beauden Barrett in support to take it and run in from 50 metres out. But the introduction of the bench allowed replacement prop Ellis Genge to run rampant in set-up play, with second five-eighths Seb Atkinson scoring the backbreaker, and replacement Marcus Smith landing two penalty goals to complete the win. Hopes of a revival by the more experienced members of the All Blacks were not met, and that is a major concern ahead of their last game of the season next week. England 37 ( Henry Slade, Jack van Poortvliet, Ben Earls, Ollie Chessum , Seb Atkinson tries;  Fin Smith 2 con;  Marcus Smith con, 2 pen) New Zealand 12 (Ethan de Groot, Beauden Barrett tries;  Damian McKenzie con). HT: 19-5

title: Man City v Fulham ratings: Anderson 8, Haaland 6; Affengruber 9, Muniz 8 - The National
content: Manchester City ended a three-game Premier League losing streak but had to settle for a frustrating home draw with Fulham on Saturday. After being beaten by Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest before the international break, the pressure was building on manager Enzo Maresca whose perfect start to the campaign was quickly turning into a distant memory. And it was looking bleak for the Italian coach when Rodrigo Muniz put the Cottagers in front after 16 minutes in front of a strangely subdued home support at the Etihad Stadium. The game's major taking point arrived later in the first-half when Erling Haaland was adjudged to have knocked the ball out of Fulham keeper Bernd Leno's grasp before bundling home what City's top-scorer thought was the leveller. England midfielder Elliot Anderson fired home an excellent volley to make it 1-1 just before the hour mark but that was to be the ned of the scoring as City's English record 20 consecutive wins over Fulham in all competitions was brought to an end with loud boos coming from home fans at the final whistle. The draw leaves City in third place, level with Brighton in second but five points shy of leaders Arsenal both of whom have yet to play this weekend. Fulham's third consecutive draw means they have now gone five matches unbeaten and are three points clear of the relegation zone. Manchester City 1-1 FulhamMan City's poor run of form continues. This 1-1 draw with Fulham means they've now won just one point in their last four games.It also means that Fulham's 20-game losing streak against Man City in all competitions is over! pic.twitter.com/UMoVGHU12I Man City goalscorer Anderson: “It's very frustrating. Going a goal down wasn't ideal but it seems to be happening. The second half was better, more intensity, we pushed higher. We just struggled to get the second goal. We're working on that [falling behind so much]. We are doing everything we can to fix it. “I was just playing a little bit higher up today – focusing on doing the best job for the team. Fighting on the ball and off the ball. That's my job on the edge of the box on corners from that side. Try to get a clean connection on target. Trying to stay calm in those situations and make good contact. “Every game we are learning things. We'll train harder. We'll be ready for the next one. It's been an interesting week [Anderson had been sent off for England last weekend].” Fulham manager Alvaro Arbeloa: "I am happy with a point but would prefer three. I'm so happy with our performance - how we played and pressed them. We came here thinking we can beat them and not just defending. We could have scored one or two more. I'm so proud of the players." "It wasn't easy [on persuading his players they could win]. After the international break it's never easy, especially coming here. I told them we lost the 20 games before, we're not playing those 20 games. "If we believe we can beat them. If we fight for every ball and play with character and personality we'll have the chance to beat them. They believed and played so well." Gianluigi Donnarumma – 8/10: No chance with Muniz goal but in right place to block Bobb shot from close range. Good saves low down from Muniz and Bassey. Booked for dissent. Needed this performance after recent struggles. Abdukodir Khusanov – 7/10: In right place to sweep up and deny Sessegnon getting in on goal in 14th minute. Good performance from Uzbekistan defender. Ruben Dias – 7/10: Captain sent header over Fulham bar from inside six-yard box although was difficult opportunity. Decent enough from City's Portuguese captain but team continues to look fragile defensively. Marc Guehi – 7/10: Missed England's games in international break due to injury but back for City. Form has been up an down this season but no repeat of recent blunders. Nico O'Reilly – 5/10: Left-back was denied early goal by Affengruber block. Caught well out of position for Muniz's early goal and his sloppiness by not playing to the whistle gifted chance to Bobb. Poor opening 45 minutes and lucky not be hooked. Better, if far from great, after break. Elliot Anderson – 8/10: Beaten by the pace of Bobb ahead of Muniz's goal. Powered home superb first-time volley on edge of area to make it 1-1 with first Premier League goal for City. Almost through on goal minutes later but lost footing. Sent another effort centimetres wide of target. Ayyoub Bouaddi – 7/10: Moroccan midfielder, making his third Premier League start, struggled to deal with Fulham's pressing in opening half. Much improved in second when he was central to much of City's best work. Phil Foden – 6/10: Back in starting XI and supplied one fine through-ball for Haaland in disappointingly quiet first half. Had goal-bound shot blocked just after break. No shock when replaced in second half. Man City's are now winless in their last four Premier League games.Next up? Arsenal 😬 pic.twitter.com/Jg2UqjNQsJ Iliman Ndiaye – 6/10: Former Everton winger produced perfect cross to set-up chance for Haaland who bundled home, but goal was disallowed. Well shackled by Sessegnon. Jermey Doku – 6/10: Hit and miss with final ball but pace and trickery always a threat. City needed a moment of magic on subdued day at Etihad but it never arrived. Erling Haaland – 6/10: Sniff of goal inside ten minutes but shot was blocked. Bundled ball home in 25th minute but disallowed for allegedly kicking ball out of Leno's hands. Wild shot over 10 minutes later. Frustrating day for the Premier League's top-scorer. Rayan Cherki (On for Foden, 70') – 5/10: No chance to make impact. Josko Gvardiol (On for O'Reilly, 78') – N/A: Surprising he was not brought on for struggling O'Reilly earlier. Bernd Leno 7/10: Can count himself lucky Haaland's goal ruled out as looked like German keeper had lost control of ball. No chance with Anderson's excellent volley. Kenny Tete 8/10: Both Fulham's full-backs had been recalled to team and both did well. Right-back Tete was tasked with dealing with Doku and did well against the Belgian. Needed rescue tackle from teammate Affengruber after his mistake allowed City in on goal. Calvin Bassey 7/10: Captain's clinical foul on Foden, who was set to launch dangerous count-attack, earned yellow card after 20 minutes. Often went deep into City half to successfully press opponents. Could have made it 2-1 to Fulham but shot saved by Donnarumma. David Affengruber 9/10: Big role in opening 10 minutes with goal-saving blocks on shots from Haaland and O'Reilly. Another excellent tackle to take ball off toes of Ndiaye. Another fine block to deflect Foden effort out for corner just after break. Outstanding from the Austrian. Ryan Sessegnon 7/10: Left-back stuck to task against tough opponent in Ndiaye keeping Senegalese's impact down to odd flashes. Shea Charles 7/10: Former City midfielder picked up booking for clumsy challenge on Anderson which sent City midfielder flying just before half-time. But should be proud of efforts, like rest of teammates, Sander Berge 7/10: A reliable presence in midfield for Fulham, keeps it simple with possession and plenty of well-timed challenges. Josh King 7/10: Midfielder, who was just called up to the senior England squad for first time, was one of those who found joy attacking down City's left flank in first-half. Alex Iwobi 7/10: Making his 100th Premier League start for Fulham but picked up very early booking for blatant foul on Anderson. Relentless in pressing of City. Oscar Bobb – 7/10: Left City for Fulham in January, Norwegian winger supplied impressive assist for Muniz's goal. Had chance to make it 2-0 just before break but Donnarumma blocked his shot. Rodrigo Muniz – 8/10: First start of season after scoring late leveller after coming on as substitute against Newcastle last time out and clipped home fine finish to make it 1-0 here. Denied second goal by good stop from Donnarumma. Antonee Robinson (On for Iwobi, 70') – 7/10: Slotted straight in with no problems. title: England v All Blacks: Five takeaways as 'wonderfully' un-English performance delivers historic victory - Planet Rugby
content: England's Seb Atkinson and an inset of Maro Itoje England produced their biggest-ever winning margin over New Zealand, a five-try, 37-12 rout at Allianz Stadium that keeps them in the hunt for next weekend’s Nations Championship final. Following England’s record-breaking 37-12 victory over the All Blacks in London, here are our five takeaways from the Nations Championship clash. England made a statement with a convincing and, at times, exhilarating 37- 12 win over New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, five tries to two, with the bonus-point wrapped up by the 43rd minute and the Hillary Shield retained, and the 25-point margin is the biggest any England side has managed against the All Blacks in 121 years of trying, comfortably eclipsing the 38-21 of 2012. Whilst England will be the first to admit they left two or three tries out there, it was the manner they played that was the most impressive thing; we are witnessing something very, very special here, an identity being crafted. This England side played with a swagger and a confidence we haven’t seen in a white shirt for some time, and it was joyous rugby, where shirt numbers don’t matter; wonderfully un-English, in other words, and one to hang up on the wall. If the wins over Japan and Australia were the pre-season nets, this was the Test match hundred, and what an innings it was. Possession against transition was the contest we expected, and possession won it by a distance. England had 64 per cent of the ball and 66 per cent of the territory, carried 100 times to New Zealand’s 50 and made 551 metres to their 267, roughly five and a half metres every time they took it up; for context, the best metre-gaining Tier 1 side of 2023, Ireland, averaged under four. England kicked 580 metres to New Zealand’s 520, coughed up fewer turnovers, conceded fewer penalties, carried further and got into the 22 far more often. The exception was rucks, 134 to 67, and that’s the interesting bit; England broke the fewest-rucks rule because every one of those rucks came with go-forward behind it, against a defence that missed 35 tackles to their nine. Before a ball was kicked, Lewis Moody, who is living with motor neurone disease, delivered the match ball to launch the My Name’5 Doddie Foundation’s FRONT UP campaign and stood with England as they faced the haka, a ritual that runs deeper than most for New Zealand captain Codie Taylor, whose own family line goes back to its originators. The All Blacks applauded Moody onto the field in front of 81,953, which was class from them in a week when class has been in short supply elsewhere. England v All Blacks, LIVE BLOG: Coverage of the Nations Championship fixture At times you’d have wondered whether the two sides had put on the wrong colour shirts, and nowhere was that clearer than in the way England’s forwards ignored the numbers on their backs. Ollie Chessum wore 6, but in defence he dropped into the second row and Alex Coles took the blindside edge, and then they swapped back when England had the ball, Chessum out in the wide channels carrying like a flanker; it’s a hybrid role, it’s been a revelation for him and for England, and on this evidence he’s one of the top three locks in the world, which is some going for a man wearing 6. He’s in there for the lineout as much as anything. England went long to Chesms at the tail time after time, four times in the first 20 minutes alone, and the long throw does two jobs at once; it takes New Zealand’s lineout forwards out of the defensive picture and it keeps their backline ten metres back until the lineout is over, so Seb Atkinson was hitting the ball at full tilt against a defence that hadn’t been allowed to come forward. Chessum was also picked to attack New Zealand’s throw, and it wobbled, an overthrow on England’s five-metre line wasting their best chance of the first quarter, and when New Zealand moved Tupou Vaa’i to the back to compete with him, Chessum took it anyway. He scored the bonus-point try two minutes after the break, Cadan Murley coming off his wing to put him away down the left touchline, and four minutes from time he absolutely atomised Scott Barrett. Then there’s Ben Earl, a seven in some eyes, playing eight and making fools of the hybrid haters all over again. He carried 32 times, a record for an England forward, for 146 metres, beat seven defenders, made two clean breaks and 15 tackles, went through on his own off the back of a scrum 18 metres out for England’s third try, and walked off with the player of the match award. When Greg Fisilau, a specialist number eight, came on, Earl stayed at 8 for his gas and Fisilau went to 7, and when Henry Pollock arrived with 14 minutes left it was on the wing in Murley’s place, where his first act was to smash Rieko Ioane and leave him counting his ribs, and his second was to start telling the backs where to stand. No shame. It’ll annoy the knuckle-draggers who don’t like shirt changes no end, but this is how the best sides in the world pick now, by what a player does, and England are finally doing it too. England player ratings v All Blacks: Ben Earl ‘fundamental’ to victory as Pom Squad ‘explode’ Lee Blackett turned 44 today, and England’s attack coach won’t get a better present. Fin Smith conducted the whole thing, 22 passes and a kick through behind a flat New Zealand line that Henry Slade scored from inside four minutes, and what’s changed in his game is the freedom; his vision and his willingness to run on and make decisions at pace, much as Antoine Dupont did against South Africa last week, is the difference between this England and the one that kicked and waited. Around him, everybody fired. Seb Atkinson was a rock, and the timing of his passing was superb, three times in the first quarter taking the ball right to the nose of the defence before slipping a short pass, and he got the try he deserved at 63 minutes after Ellis Genge folded New Zealand in half down the middle with two enormous carries. Slade looks rejuvenated, and his kick ahead and regather set up Jack van Poortvliet’s try just after the half-hour; George Furbank was a creative genius at full-back, from the 50:22 in the eighth minute to the burst down the middle that started that same score; and Murley, only in the side because Tommy Freeman pulled out with a thigh injury before kick-off, was quick, brave and everywhere, with three defenders beaten and two dominant tackles to go with the Chessum try. England’s USP is gas, gas and more gas, and Will Joseph, moved to the right wing, added 61 metres. Van Poortvliet put boot to ball 17 times for 354 metres and Furbank three times for 102, and between them, with Smith’s kicks through, short and long, England kicked nothing loose all afternoon, so New Zealand’s counter-attackers spent the day catching the ball with white shirts already in their faces. Codie Taylor told me this week that New Zealand had been “punched in the nose early” in Cardiff, and that the lesson was the importance of starting well over here. Four minutes in, Slade was over. By half-time it was 19-5, and by the end New Zealand had made 237 tackles to England’s 119 and missed 26 of them, which says plenty about how little ball they had. There was no power and no carrying in midfield; the attack was so lateral it barely threatened the gainline, they lost nearly every collision, and for long spells the strategy appeared to be to give it to Wallace Sititi and hope; Sititi made 25 tackles and carried 11 times, and deserved better. The defence on Earl’s try was straight out of a primary school playground; Cam Roigard and Peter Lakai both left grasping at thin air, though Lakai, with 18 tackles and two turnovers, was otherwise the one All Black who looked like himself. What pressure they did build, they undid themselves with an off-the-ball tackle from Damian McKenzie and a collapsed maul from Scott Barrett among ten penalties conceded, whilst England’s defence was suffocating for most of the afternoon. Maro Itoje was titanic, smashing bodies, a nause of the highest order and a relentless bore for detail who never let New Zealand settle, and he was maybe fortunate when he hit Tupou Vaa’i in the second half, though both men were so low that Nic Berry called it a rugby incident. New Zealand’s one transition score came at 51 minutes, Roigard timing his pass to perfection for Beauden Barrett to score on his 150th Test, which makes him only the fourth man, and the first back, to reach that number. It was about the only thing they had to cheer. Two defeats in eight days, to Wales and now this, leave Dave Rennie with a long week of questions. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. If there’s a blot, England left two or three tries out there, Ben Curry held up over the line in the first half and another chance gone begging in the final ten minutes; they gave away a penalty in the air at a restart just before the break that ended in Ethan de Groot’s maul try; and Fletcher Newell had the better of Fin Baxter twice at the scrum, Baxter binding too short, before Will Stuart evened things up late on by melting George Bower. For a side striving for perfection, they’ll be livid about all of it. So, what happens next? The bonus point leaves England on 25 points, and France need a try-bonus win over Argentina in Paris tonight to go past them; anything les s and England top the northern conference on a points difference France can’t realistically catch. New Zealand are stuck on 22, and any South African win over Ireland in Dublin this afternoon takes the Springboks above them. That leaves a tantalising possibility. If France miss out on their bonus point and Ireland beat South Africa, England and New Zealand meet again in the final at Allianz Stadium next Sunday; if France get it and the Springboks win, the two meet in the second-place match on Saturday instead. Either way, England would get the chance to beat New Zealand three times in a row, something they’ve never done. Lewis Moody will have been pleased, mind you; the afternoon started with a world-class back-rower and finished with another taking the POM award. title: England player ratings v All Blacks: Ben Earl 'fundamental' to victory as Pom Squad 'explode' - Planet Rugby
content: Ben Earl (right) and Greg Fisilau (left) were among the key performers for England v All Blacks Following England’s win over the All Blacks at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham, here is how we scored Steve Borthwick’s side from the Nations Championship Test. 15 George Furbank: Showed no signs of rust after returning from a groin issue, with yet another brilliant effort. His early 50:22, taken on the run and under pressure, was simply jaw-dropping; but away from that, his dual playmaking and running threat just added a lovely dynamic to this attack and ultimately helped get them over the line, and one that surely cements his place at the top of the depth chart once more. 8 14 Will Joseph: While he didn’t bag five tries today, he looked every inch a Test star in a fine shift. Made something happen whenever he was given the ball, churning through metres he didn’t have a right to make considering the defenders clinging onto him, and consistently put his hand up for carries. A nice way to continue his England return. 7 13 Henry Slade: Another really nice effort from Slade this autumn, as he continues to dismiss any doubts over the long-term future of the 13 shirt. Began the afternoon with a nice try, and carried on from there with some lovely flashes ball-in-hand; namely the solo break-and-kick in the build-up to Jack van Poortvliet’s score. One of a number of exquisite displays from this England backline. 8 12 Seb Atkinson: Like fellow injury returner Furbank, did not look like he’d spent a week on the physio table. His delicious, deft handling got the England attack purring, combining well with both F. Smith and Slade in the process, and added some serious heft when used as a punch runner. His try felt like a real turning point in the Test, coming at a time where England were looking to kill it off. 8 11 Cadan Murley: Chucked in at the last minute following an injury to Tommy Freeman, but goodness me did he take his chance. Seemed to have the All Blacks defence on strings at times ball-in-hand, carving it up with pretty much every touch of the ball and making things happen for the rest of his side in the process. Showed exactly what he can do in Tests like this, which will please Borthwick no end. 8 10 Fin Smith: He will be frustrated at the missed conversions, but that shouldn’t take away from what was a really nice display. His link-up with the rest of the backline and desire to play up-tempo played a huge role in getting England on the front-foot early doors, and his assist for Slade’s opener deserves some flowers. 8 9 Jack van Poortvliet: Took a conductor’s role today, and seemed to relish it. Kicked well when called upon, injected tempo into the play wherever possible and got a real tune out of the backline in the process. 7 England v All Blacks: Five takeaways as ‘wonderfully’ un-English performance delivers historic victory 8 Ben Earl: You do start to run out of superlatives to describe Ben Earl in an England shirt, who was once again outstanding. He really seemed to grab the Test by the scruff of the jersey, making barnstorming carry after barnstorming carry and ending with a record-breaking 32 carries for 146, all while grabbing a nice try for his efforts. Was just a fundamental part of this victory. 9 7 Ben Curry: Complimented the rest of the back-row superbly well all afternoon, which in turn allowed the others to flourish. Rolled up his sleeves and went looking for work in the breakdown, as well as getting stuck into the battle in the loose. 7 Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. 6 Ollie Chessum: Probably his best outing in an England shirt yet, which is some doing considering his efforts to date. Owned every little moment he was involved in, be it at the lineout, defence or his nice role in attack as the wide forward, and that helped drive his side home in the end. His try was richly deserved too. 9 5 Alex Coles: Will be very sore tomorrow after an industrious effort. As we’ve come to expect, ran his blood to water in the tight as he did all the ugly, nitty-gritty work to get his side playing on the front-foot. 7 4 Maro Itoje (c): Proper captain’s knock from the skipper, who continues to excel in this Nations Championship block. Had the bit properly between his teeth in an unrelenting effort up-front, and played his role well in the lineout. 8 3 Joe Heyes: Fared slightly better than his prop partner in the scrum, with tightheads very much getting the edge in their respective battles, and chucked himself about in defence as per. Solid. 6 2 Jamie George: England’s lineout was top-notch all afternoon, and he was at the heart of his with his pinpoint throwing. Got involved in the loose too, which rounded off a nice afternoon’s work. 7 1 Fin Baxter: Given a hard time in the scrum for the majority of his shift, but did look to get around the park wherever possible. 5 Replacements: The tone for the bench was set when George Martin came on and banged an All Black carrier with his first involvement, but the bench simply exploded. The initially-deployed grouping of Martin, Ellis Genge, Luke Cowan-Dickie, Greg Fisilau and Will Stuart made an immediate difference in the second-half, while Henry Pollock, Marcus Smith and Ben Spencer all had some nice involvements too. The Pom Squad is looking an increasingly big part of England’s gameplan now, and long may that continue. 8 READ MORE: Ireland v Springboks, LIVE BLOG: Coverage of the Nations Championship fixture © Planet Sport Limited 2026 • All Rights Reserved

title: GTA VI Sales Just Blew GTA V Sales Out of the Water - Newser
content: Sales of Grand Theft Auto VI generated a record with $3.79 billion in first-day retail sales, maker Rockstar Games said on Friday, underscoring the enormous demand for the first new installment in the blockbuster series in 13 years. The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of Thursday, the day the game launched, per the AP. Rockstar also said in a release that it sold 32.5 million units prerelease, setting a record across platforms. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world," Sam Houser, Rockstar's president, said in a release. For context, Grand Theft Auto V, released in 2013, generated $1 billion in retail sales in its first three days and went on to become one of the bestselling video games of all time, accounting for more than 230 million of the franchise's 470 million-plus units sold globally, per publisher Take-Two Interactive. Earlier Friday, market research firm Sensor Tower estimated GTA VI had generated $2.36 billion in revenue on approximately 24.6 million units sold. Rockstar's figures, released later in the day, were based on the company's own estimates of worldwide, day-one retail sales. Earlier this month, the PlayStation blog said that GTA VI was the most preordered game in the history of its namesake store. The game's release also ended years of secrecy around its cast. In terms of the two main characters, Manni L. Perez plays Lucia, while Dylan Rourke portrays Jason. Bobby Moynihan, Stephen Root, Taryn Manning, Roselyn Sanchez, and rapper Denzel Curry are among the other thespian names in Rockstar's sprawling credits. The enormous launch comes after more than a decade of anticipation around a series that has become one of the biggest properties in entertainment. Copyright 2026 Newser, LLC. All rights reserved. title: Confirmed Arsenal Team v Newcastle: Guimarães Starts With Havertz Up Front - Yahoo Sports
content: Arsenal return to Premier League action this evening as they take on Newcastle United at St James' Park, with kick-off scheduled for 5.30pm UK time. After the international break, the Gunners will be looking to pick up where they left off and maintain their impressive start to the campaign. Mikel Arteta's side have built their title challenge on defensive resilience, consistency and an ability to find a way to win even when they aren't at their attacking best. But St James' Park is rarely an easy place to visit, and Newcastle will be determined to make life difficult for the league leaders. Mikel Arteta has handed Bruno Guimarães a starting place on his return to St James' Park, where he faces his former club for the first time since joining Arsenal in the summer. With Martin Zubimendi sidelined through injury, the Brazilian partners Declan Rice in midfield, while Martin Odegaard captains the Gunners. It promises to be an emotional occasion for Guimarães, but his experience of Newcastle and their home crowd could prove invaluable this evening. At the back, Ezri Konsa retains his place alongside Gabriel, with William Saliba is on the bench after Arteta confirmed his fitness ahead of the game. Kai Havertz gets the nod over Viktor Gyokeres up front, supported by Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze. With Manchester City having dropped points against Fulham earlier today, Arsenal have another opportunity to strengthen their position at the top of the Premier League. title: Incredible number of Newcastle United v Arsenal tickets still on sale on Saturday afternoon - Yahoo Sports
content: I thought I would have a look just in case, see if by chance any Newcastle United v Arsenal tickets were available on Saturday afternoon. Just in case you aren't aware, the club allow Newcastle United season ticket holders to sell their tickets for individual Premier League games. This was a very positive move by the club as it means that seats don't need to be left empty if a season ticket holder is ill for example. Using the online club system, season ticket holders can make their ticket available for a league match, with Newcastle United members then able to go onto the NUFC official ticketing site (you have to be then logged in as a member to see the tickets that are available) to buy. The club also make money from this. As I understand it, the fan (season ticket holder) selling the ticket is credited with the pro rata match price of their season ticket and if the ticket is then bought by a member, they are charged the far higher single ticket price, with the club banking the difference. As a member, I had no luck in the ballot for Newcastle United v Arsenal tickets. The demand was huge, I had a ridiculously high number for the queue sale and stood no chance, along with countless thousands of other Newcastle United members. Anyway, I have just went onto the club's ticketing site (just before 2pm on Saturday) and I couldn't believe how many Newcastle United v Arsenal tickets were on sale! To be honest, I wasn't expecting there to be any, I was just looking in the vain hope I might hit very lucky. What I found was I had a choice of all aroundSt James' Park! All four stands with plenty tickets up for sale from season ticket holders. I snapped up a couple for me and my mate for the East Stand and after sending this article into The Mag I will be heading off to the Toon to meet up with the lads (mostly season ticket holders) for some pre-match refreshments. After buying our tickets I counted up all the Newcastle United v Arsenal tickets that season ticket holders are trying to sell and there were 147 available (it had been 149 I guess before I snapped up ours). Apologies for my wonky photography skills but the red areas are where there were Newcastle United v Arsenal tickets available just over three and a half hours before the match… I am over the moon getting these tickets but at the same time absolutely stunned that so many season ticket holders are trying to flog their tickets. Is it because they will get too upset seeing Bruno Guimaraes in an Arsenal shirt? Anyway, if you are a member who didn't get a ticket for today's match, log onto the official ticketing site and take your pick!!

title: Man City 1-1 Fulham: How the players rated - BBC
content: Elliot Anderson scored his second goal of the season for Manchester City Elliot Anderson's stunning second-half volley rescued a point against Fulham, but Manchester City extend their winless run to four games in the Premier League. Here's how I rated the players, and how you rated the players. Gianluigi Donnarumma: Has been in poor form recently but could do nothing about the opener. Made a very important save to deny Rodrigo Muniz. 6 Abdukodir Khusanov: Not a natural right-back and noticeable at times, cutting back instead of marauding forward with ball at his feet. 6 Ruben Dias: Another game where captain Dias and his side have failed to keep a clean sheet. 6 Marc Guehi: Missed England's recent matches through injury but did not look in any trouble in this game. 7 Nico O'Reilly: Almost scored at one end and could have given one away at the other when he tried to play for offside. 6 Ayyoub Bouaddi: Given a start in place of Enzo Fernandez and grew in the second half but was he able to fully grasp his opportunity? 7 Elliot Anderson: The pick of the home players when his side needed him the most. Covered every blade of grass and equalised with a sensational volley. 9 Iliman Ndiaye: Needs to start stepping up. Created very little and hasn't really shone in the absence of Antoine Semenyo. 6 Jeremy Doku: Another who has to start performing. Did very little of note here and was penalised for a foul throw when chasing a winner. Unforgivable. 6 Phil Foden: Showed flashes of his talent but not enough to influence the game. 6 Erling Haaland: Had a goal in the first half disallowed and blazed another decent opportunity over. 6 Bernd Leno: Made some routine saves but Anderson's strike was past him in a flash. 6 Kenny Tete: Solid at right-back, keeping Doku in check. 7 Calvin Bassey: The captain has been linked with a move to Manchester United and was a solid presence in the heart of the backline. 6 David Affengruber: The Austrian made a couple of crucial blocks to deny certain goals. 7 Ryan Sessegnon: Decent performance against the tricky Ndiaye. 6 Sander Berge: Shielded his back four superbly for much of the game in an impressive showing. 7 Alex Iwobi: Booked in the opening five minutes but recovered well. 6 Oscar Bobb: Returned to City and provided the assist for the first goal. 7 Shea Charles: Steady but unspectacular showing for another player against his former club. 6 Josh King: Earned a call-up to England recently and was lively in the final third. 7 Rodrigo Muniz: Marvellous curled effort to open the scoring. 8 After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: MW11 VAR decisions explained: Why Haaland goal v Fulham did not stand - Premier League
content: See the latest interventions by VAR as explained by the Premier League Match Centre X account This article collates the X posts of the Premier League Match Centre which provides explanations for decisions made by the referees and Video Assistant Referees (VAR) in Premier League matches. Incident - 25min Manchester City striker Erling Haaland gets on the end of a cross, shooting towards goal. Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno stops the shot with this hands, but Haaland follows up to kick the ball from between Leno's hands into the goal. The referee Tom Bramall indicated that Haaland had fouled Leno. The Premier League Match Centre X post said: "The referee’s call of free-kick to Fulham and no goal to Manchester City was checked and confirmed by VAR – with the goalkeeper deemed to be in control of the ball. "VAR: 'The ball is in control between both hands and then is played out of that possession by the attacker, and then into the back of the net.'" IFAB's Law 12 states: "A goalkeeper is considered to be in control of the ball with their hand(s)/arm(s) when: • the ball is between their hands/arms or between their hand(s)/arm(s) and any surface (e.g. ground, own body) • holding the ball in their outstretched open hand(s) • bouncing it on the ground or throwing it in the air"A goalkeeper cannot be challenged by an opponent when in control of the ball with their hand(s)/arm(s)." title: Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing review — ‘I adored driving this American car’ - The Times
content:
I used to go to America a lot and I never enjoyed myself there. There were too many state laws, you weren’t allowed to cross the road, smoking made you a pariah and if you asked for a second bottle of wine over lunch, the waitress would faint. I also couldn’t bear the way that when you got off the plane there was always a traffic jam of wheelchairs to ferry the fat people to the luggage collection zone. And I hated their tomatoes, which were the size of grapefruits and cost only five cents but tasted of nothing at all. I also hated their hotel rooms because the bedspread was always burgundy and you could never sleep, partly because you were constantly being electrocuted by the nylon sheets but mostly because of the incessant chuntering from the ice machine in the corridor. And the speed limit was a preposterous 55mph, except on the Blue Ridge Parkway where it was 20mph. As a result of all this and more, I used to sink to my knees and kiss the ground when I landed back at Heathrow as it felt as if I was returning to a free country from what felt like a big, hot prison full of nutcases and slow-moving idiots. However, today it’s the other way round. I’ve been to the States three times in the past six months, and on each occasion it has felt as if I’ve arrived in a country that’s mostly working from a country that sort of isn’t. You can eat well in America now and you can stay in hotels where the furniture is tasteful. In Boston I saw people walking to work, in Miami I watched a game of actual football and in Austin, at Joe Rogan’s comedy club, there were performers on the stage smoking. I met with state officials who were helpful, found bars that were beautiful, and on an early morning walk round a city centre lake saw not one scrap of litter, bit of graffiti or tramp. I encountered people who knew where Europe was and that Africa isn’t a country. I was offered rosé wine. And thanks to Global Entry, I didn’t have to wait in line for three hours to be scowled at by an uninterested border force person. Which I sure as hell have to do when I go to Italy or France. This brings me neatly to the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing. Let’s start first of all with that name. Renault and Nissan tell us that they have to use stupid made-up words such as Kadjar and Qashqai because everything that’s an actual word has already been trademarked by someone else. So how come no one had bagged “Blackwing”? Because that’s about the coolest name we’ve seen in cardom since the Jensen Interceptor went west. Of course, the Americans have always been as good at finding car names as they were bad at making cars. You may look back with rose-tinted fondness at the Corvette Stingray, the ’67 Ford Mustang and the Camaro SS (not the best choice of name). But while these muscle cars were childishly endearing, they were also pretty awful to drive. All American cars were, from those Lincolns that were still rocking back and forth on their suspension when you got back to them after a trip to the cinema, to their hopeless attempts to get sensible. AMC Pacer? Pontiac Aztek? I mean come on. It was all just a desert of cheap fabrics, burgundy upholstery and unnecessarily large engines that produced about four horsepower. But like I say, America has changed in recent years and so it seems have the cars because, crikey, this Blackwing is a handsome brute. And it appears to be well put together too. The shut lines are very Japanese and the stitching on the seats is kind of Rolls-Royce-ish. The engine, though, is still quite old-skool. It may have lightweight titanium valves, forged connecting rods and pistons, but there is no hybrid drive and no turbocharging. It’s just a big pushrod 6.2-litre supercharged V8 — an engine last used in the old Corvette C7 Z06. I think that’s the point they’re trying to make: “We are being forced to go electric but, hey guys, this is what we are leaving behind.” It’s a lot. Because this car produces 668 brake horsepower and a mountain of torque, which means you can go from 0-62mph in 3.6 seconds and then onwards to a top speed of 205mph. This, then, is a very real, very serious rival to the BMW M5. Which is quite ambitious for a company that’s spent its entire life making either slab-sided blancmanges for Tin Men or presidential SUVs. Now they’re in Formula 1 and going after the best sports saloon of them all. And I’m not going to beat about the bush. They’ve pretty much done it. Let’s start with some niggles. The door mirrors are too small. The turning circle is woeful and thanks to a combination of great thirst and a small tank, its effective range is just 200 miles. But now let’s move on to the good stuff and we shall start with the price. In America it’s the equivalent of £75,000, which means it’s two thirds of the price of an M5. And is it only two thirds of the car? Well, I like the fact that, in basic form, this is rear-wheel drive. I also liked the manual gearbox. Certainly I liked it more than the valet parkers at my hotel did — they had literally no idea what it was. I know a clutch is a faff in town but on the open road, with the rev match facility employed to, er, match the revs on down changes, it was like being in a proper car. And a fast one. But it wasn’t the speed that impressed me most, it was the refinement. It was superbly quiet and civilised, and the ride was sublime. And God almighty, the brakes were good. I adored driving this car. It steers properly, hangs on in the bends and stops like it’s hit a tree. My only real gripe is that aside from the Blackwing handle, it feels and looks a bit too European. I wish it sounded a bit more like the American V8s of old — a noise AA Gill once described as two lesbians in a bucket. And a little chrome wouldn’t go amiss. Just a nod to the automotive history of the country where it was made. But maybe the American dream these days is to be a bit more European. To offer rosé wine and have Bamford shampoo in hotel rooms and not talk in lifts. Maybe that’s why I’ve started to like the place. Maybe America is becoming what Europe used to be before it all went wrong. Footnote. Please do not think this piece is some kind of love letter to Donald Trump. I don’t think he’s responsible for any of the changes in America because he is a revolting man. © Times Media Limited 2025.Registered in England No. 894646. Registered office: 1 London Bridge Street, SE1 9GF.
