title: The Relationship Between IHL and Genocide in The Gambia v. Myanmar Case - Opinio Juris
content: In association with the International Commission of Jurists Much has already been written on the ICJ’s landmark judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar case (GvM), and much more will no doubt be written in the coming days. In this post, I want to focus on how the Court dealt with a specific — and admittedly narrow — issue I recently addressed in an article in the Journal of International Criminal Justice: whether genocide can be committed through acts that comply with IHL, such as killing a combatant who is a member of a protected group. Neither of the ICJ’s two previous genocide decisions, Bosnia v. Serbia and Croatia v. Serbia, specifically resolved that issue. They did, however, suggest that genocide could potentially be committed through IHL-compliant acts. In the Bosnia case, the Court rejected Serbia’s argument that it could not be found responsible for genocide because its deportation of the Bosniaks complied with IHL, noting in para. 334 that “no such justification could be accepted in the face of proof of specific intent.” In the Croatia case, the Court did not address the genocide issue directly, but acknowledged in para. 474 that because “a particular act may be perfectly lawful under one body of legal rules and unlawful under another… it cannot be excluded in principle that an act carried out during an armed conflict and lawful under international humanitarian law can at the same time constitute a violation by the State in question of some other international obligation incumbent upon it.” There is no equivocation in GvM. On the contrary, the majority explicitly rejected the idea that that genocide cannot be committed through acts that comply with IHL: 305. Accordingly, the Court concludes that although compliance with another body of international law, including international humanitarian law, may inform the identification of intent with respect to the actus reus of genocide, as well as genocidal intent, such compliance does not exclude conduct from the scope of the Genocide Convention. The majority’s analysis is extremely brief — barely two paragraphs. The first paragraph (303) simply notes, with regard to the actus reus of genocide, that “[t]he text of Article II of the Convention does not require that the acts enumerated therein be unlawful pursuant to a distinct body of international law.” The second paragraph (304), which addresses genocide’s mens rea, is a bit more substantive, pointing out that although compliance with IHL is relevant to the existence of specific intent, IHL-compliance and specific intent can nevertheless coexist in the same act: With respect to genocidal intent, the Court likewise has considered that compliance or non-compliance with international humanitarian law, including whether attacks “caused casualties and damage far in excess of what was justified by military necessity”, may be relevant in inferring the presence or absence of the specific intent to commit genocide. On the other hand, the fact that members of a protected group could be lawfully targeted or incidentally harmed under international humanitarian law does not exclude the possibility that they may be killed or harmed with genocidal intent (citation omitted). None of the other opinions and declarations in the case conclude either that an IHL-compliant act cannot satisfy the actus reus of genocide or question the idea that an IHL-compliant act could be committed with specific intent. Indeed, in his partly concurring and partly dissenting separate opinion, Judge ad hoc Kress provided a useful scenario that demonstrates why it would make little sense to exclude IHL-compliant acts from the scope of the Genocide Convention: Imagine a case where a State has formed genocidal intent and has begun to realize it through acts of killings against members of the targeted protected group. Now imagine that members of that group organize themselves militarily and fight back in defence of the group in such a manner that the threshold of a non-international armed conflict is reached. I would find it difficult to accept that, in such a case, the killings of fighters of the newly formed military wing of the protected group cease to qualify as acts within the meaning of Article II (a) of the Genocide Convention merely because these acts do not violate the targeting rules applicable under the law of non-international armed conflict. For this would mean that the State concerned could — to that extent — carry out its genocidal plan without thereby committing genocide, simply because the targeted group succeeded in organizing itself militarily in its defence. The scenario assumes, of course, that we know the state in question specifically intends to destroy the protected group. There will obviously be situations in which it is unclear whether a state using violence against members of a protected group intends to destroy the group or is acting pursuant to non-genocidal motivations. When that is the case, it may be difficult — perhaps impossible — to infer specific intent from acts that comply with IHL. Indeed, it may even be difficult to infer specific intent from acts that violate IHL. Sometimes a war crime is just a war crime. The basic point, however, remains: when the specific intent to destroy a group can be proven, there is no reason to consider acts of violence against members of that group to be non-genocidal simply because they complied with IHL. On that point, the majority in GvM and Judge ad hoc Kress are absolutely right. Kevin Jon Heller is Professor of International Law and Security at the University of Copenhagen's Centre for Military Studies. He was Special Adviser to the ICC Prosecutor on War Crimes from 2021-2026. ©  Opinio Juris | Design by Open & Honest | In association with the International Commission of Jurists

title: 'We know what this game means' - Virgil van Dijk previews Liverpool v Man Utd - Liverpool FC
content: Virgil van Dijk is well versed in the rivalry between Liverpool and Manchester United - and the captain cannot wait to be part of it again this weekend. Following the international break, the Reds return to action against Mauricio Pochettino’s United at Anfield on Sunday afternoon (4.30pm GMT kick-off). Van Dijk previews the game in his notes for the  matchday programme, writing: “After two weeks without Premier League football, we could not have a more exciting fixture with which to return to action. “Some of the most memorable games I have been involved in as a Liverpool player have been against Manchester United, and I am looking forward to another special Anfield atmosphere. “These are the games everyone wants to be involved in. I don’t need to talk too much about the history and the rivalry between the two clubs, I just know that you guys will be as excited as we players are to get out there and go to work. “It will be a tough game, no doubt about that. We know we are facing a team with a new manager, a team that will be highly motivated to perform, and we need to be ready to work extremely hard if we want to come away with the result we all want. “We went into the break on the back of a good, and important, away win against Crystal Palace, in which I believe we showed a lot of the qualities and characteristics required if we are to have a successful season. Inside: Crystal Palace 1-3 Liverpool | BEST away end scenes! Premier League “It wasn’t a perfect performance, by any means, but the way we stuck together, fought for everything and defended as a team for 90-plus minutes was pleasing, especially at the end of a testing run of games. “Those are the standards we need to maintain going forward. I say it so often, but the best teams are the ones who can stay consistent, week after week. We are still working towards that, and Sunday is another good test in that regard, with more big games on the horizon. “This is the busiest period of the season, without a doubt. Between now and the end of January we will play at least 19 games across four competitions, and that is something that everyone needs to be ready for. The demands are big but so are the rewards, and everyone inside the dressing room is ready for the challenges ahead. “First and foremost, though, our focus is on Sunday. We know what this game means to the club, means to you all. We know how much you will all be up for it, and I can assure you that we will be too. “Hopefully we can give you all another day to remember.” Pick up your copy of the programme at Anfield on Sunday or order from our online store

title: Liverpool v Manchester United: 13 stats to know ahead of Anfield clash - Liverpool FC
content: See the pre-match statistics to know ahead of Liverpool's hosting of Manchester United in the Premier League on Sunday. Andoni Iraola's side return to action following the November international break with a fixture against the Red Devils at Anfield. Check out key facts and figures about the encounter below… The last 11 Premier League meetings between Liverpool and United have seen 44 goals scored, with both sides netting in four of the previous five clashes. Cody Gakpo has scored more Premier League goals versus United than he has against any other opponent (five), netting in each of his last three appearances. This is the latest into a league season (matchday 11) that the clubs have met with one of them in the relegation zone since 1972-73, when bottom side United beat league leaders Liverpool 2-0 at Old Trafford in November. Liverpool's 10 BEST Premier League wins against Manchester United! This will be Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge of United – the first-ever manager to see his first league match with the club come against Liverpool. Just one of United's last nine managers (including caretakers) has lost his first Premier League game of a spell in charge of the club (won four, drawn four). Virgil van Dijk is set to start a 50th consecutive Premier League game for the Reds, which would be the fourth time he has had a run of 50+ unbroken starts in the competition – the joint-most by an outfield player, along with Sylvain Distin. Aged 35 years and 137 days, Van Dijk would also become the oldest outfield player to start 50+ consecutive Premier League games for a single club, overtaking Kevin Davies for Bolton Wanderers (67 in a row aged 34 years and 175 days). United are yet to win a Premier League away game this season (drawn three, lost two) and could lose successively on the road for the first time since September 2025. After winning this fixture last season, United are aiming for successive league wins at Anfield for the first time since January 2016 under Louis van Gaal. Pochettino has won just one of his eight previous Premier League matches against Liverpool at Anfield (drawn two, lost five), coming in his first visit with Southampton in September 2013 (1-0). In the Premier League, Pochettino has lost more games to the Reds than any other side (eight), with his lowest points per game also coming against them (0.88 – minimum five matches). Milos Kerkez could make his 50th start for Liverpool across all competitions. After 218 previous meetings between the clubs, the cumulative goals tally stands at 294 for the Reds and 296 for United.

title: Liverpool v Manchester United: Team news - Liverpool FC
content: Andoni Iraola expects to have increased options to choose from when Liverpool host Manchester United on Sunday. Jeremie Frimpong and Ryan Gravenberch are both back in training after injury lay-offs and in contention for the Premier League fixture. Head coach Iraola also confirmed Reds captain Virgil van Dijk is fit – having withdrawn from international duty last week – and there is no concern regarding Dominik Szoboszlai. At his pre-match press conference on Friday, the boss said: “Ryan Gravenberch, it’s a matter of pain, he’s managing the situation a little bit but he has been training with us the last two days. So, I hope he is available. “Jeremie is recovering. The international break sometimes helps with these things, we have introduced him with the rest of the group and he also should be available. “And Virgil also is fine to go. [Szoboszlai] is in a good place, he has trained normally. He was not strapped today. He is fine.” Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni have this week taken further steps in their long-term recoveries by participating in sessions. Neither is yet in contention for selection, however. Iraola explained: “They have to be loaded carefully – they don’t train every day with us. One day, yes. The next day, not. The next day, yes. “We are in the last part of this process, a long process. But both of them are looking good and I hope they can play in some weeks.” Hugo Ekitike remains sidelined as he undertakes rehabilitation for an Achilles rupture in April. Alexis Mac Allister is a yellow card away from receiving a one-match suspension in the Premier League. United travel to Anfield for the 4.30pm GMT kick-off having made a change in their dugout. Mauricio Pochettino was appointed as Michael Carrick’s replacement at the helm during the international break. The Argentinian will be able to call upon compatriot Lisandro Martinez, who fulfilled a one-match suspension last time out. Patrick Dorgu and Harry Maguire are also likely to be in contention – both have trained this week after prior issues. United’s injury list includes Carlos Baleba, Karl Darlow, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko, Luke Shaw and Manuel Ugarte. “There are some injured players and another player that we need to assess,” said Pochettino. “[On Saturday] we will have a better idea of the squad that will be available to travel to Liverpool.” Ahead of his first match in charge, Pochettino said: “We are so excited to be here. I think that it is an amazing club. “Yes, we are happy; at the same time, so busy. We’ve been adapting in the last few days and I think it’s a race to arrive in condition to be competitive against Liverpool, and now our focus is 100 per cent in Liverpool in the game of Sunday. “It is important to have an impact, a positive impact. You can have also a different impact, but I think to try to be positive and to create a positive impact, that is our most important job. “It is to try to get the best from [the players], to create the environment for them to express their talent, because we have talented players in the squad. That is our main focus.” Crystal Palace 1-3 Liverpool (November 8): Alisson, Araujo, Jacquet, Van Dijk, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Szoboszlai, Wirtz, Gakpo, Barcola, Isak.
